papers.abstract: The local three-dimensional (3D) atomic structure of materials and molecules can be interrogated by X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), a powerful analytical technique. Here, we introduce a diffusionmodel-based approach that rapidly infers candidate 3D structures from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data. The method is validated on multi-element hard X-ray XAS datasets and generalizes across a broad range of molecular and material systems without imposing restrictions on the number of constituent element types. Compared with multi-round iterative optimization methods for 3D structure determination that use a structure-to-spectrum model as the core spectral calculation engine, our approach substantially improves data analysis efficiency, enabling 3D structure determination within a few reverse diffusion steps. On low-end consumer GPUs, 3D structure analysis takes 0.5–5s. We anticipate that this method will significantly facilitate online data analysis at beamlines and associated real-time experimental planning and optimization, enable batch screening of atomic-level 3D structures, and improve the efficiency of conventional 3D structure fitting.
papers.title: 3D Structure Analysis from XAS using Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.
papers.title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development

papers.abstract: Diffusion models form the bulk of generative frameworks used in de novo molecular design, yet the literature remains fragmented across model formulations, molecular representations, and generative tasks, and inadequate systematic accounts exist of how these models are steered towards molecules with desired properties, an aspect of drug discovery that is paramount to acceptance. We present a scoping review of diffusion-based neural networks applied in de novo drug discovery between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) protocol, we categorise the literature into non-mutually exclusive themes covering methodological contributions, conditioning mechanisms, molecular representations, symmetries, and multi-modal integrations, and outline the datasets and evaluation metrics used throughout. Three findings emerge. First, diffusion did not displace earlier architectures so much as absorb them: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Autoencoders, and Transformers persist as backbones, and what changed was the training objective. Second, conditioning strategies reduce to structural anchoring, target-aware biochemical conditioning, property-driven steering, and multimodal latent conditioning; within these, the point in the reverse trajectory at which a conditioning signal is applied is a design variable distinct from the signal itself. Third, evaluation remains unstandardised across frameworks, datasets, and definitions. We identify the resulting gaps in controllability and interpretability as the central open challenge for conditioned molecular generation and outline the direction to ease them as this would enable generation of molecules that match the preferred property profiles.
papers.title: A Scoping Review of Diffusion-Based De Novo Molecular Generation: Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges for Computational Drug Discovery

papers.abstract: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries offer high theoretical capacity, but polysulfide dissolution and shuttling cause rapid capacity fade. Nitrogen functional groups can anchor polysulfides, yet in our previous work, introducing them through a post-carbonization cyclized-PAN treatment sacrificed much of the carbon nanofiber (CNF) mesoporosity, and Nfunctionalizing both cathode and interlayer performed worst. Here, nitrogen is introduced during fiber formation by adding urea to a PAN/PMMA precursor before gas-assisted electrospinning, followed by stabilization, carbonization, and CO2 activation. This gives N-doped mesoporous CNFs with better control over the balance between nitrogen content and pore structure. Across four cathode/interlayer combinations ,every cell with at least one N-doped component outperformed the undoped cell. The N-doped cathode with N-doped interlayer performed best, delivering 1271 mAh g-1 at 2C with the lowest charge-transfer resistance (8 Ω vs. 11 Ω undoped). Post-mortem XPS revealed Li-N interactions and polysulfide retention, strongest in the interlayers. Precursor-level nitrogen doping is therefore an effective route to Li-S cathodes and interlayers that balance nitrogen and mesoporosity.
papers.title: Facile Nitrogen Doping of Electrospun Mesoporous Carbon Nanofibers via Urea Addition for Polysulfide-Confining Li-S Cathodes and Interlayers

papers.abstract: Alkene homologation represents an efficient strategy for upgrading commodity olefins and expediting the synthesis of their longer homologues. However, current alkene homologation methodologies are limited to the access to terminal alkenes. Herein, we report a radical‑based approach that enables C2 homologation of alkenes with programmable substitution patterns. This transformation features a radical hydro-alkylation of alkenes using bromomethylphosphonium hexafluorophosphate as an electrophilic carbon radical precursor. The resulting phosphonium salt, bearing a C1-extended chain, undergoes Wittig olefination with inexpensive aldehyde/ketone to deliver C2-elongated terminal/1,2-/1,1,2-substituted alkenes (>40 examples, up to 99% yield; Z/E up to >20:1, with photocatalytic access to the E-isomers). This protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is applicable to the late-stage modification of bioactive compounds, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystals. Furthermore, by iteratively combining this C2 method with our previously established C1 homologation, the olefinic chains of complex molecules can be precisely elongated by three, four, or more carbon atoms. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including DFT calculations and experimental probes, support a radical pathway and identify hydrogen bonding between HFIP and triethylamine, which raises the competing HAT barrier from 8.5 to 13.1 kcal/mol, as the key element that suppresses reductive debromination and channels the radical toward C–C bond formation.
papers.title: C2 Homologation of Alkenes with Programmable Substitution

papers.abstract: Decentralized alternatives to centralized fertilizer production are needed to reduce supply chain risks, minimize transportation costs, and lower environmental impacts. Solar-powered Electrochemical Stripping (ECS) is an emerging technology that can produce ammonium fertilizer in a distributed manner through wastewater nitrogen recovery. We quantify the fraction of fertilizer demand in the United States that can be met by a wastewater feedstock while minimizing transportation distances, finding that 55% (5.54 Mt N per year) of demand is co-located with sufficient supply from domestic, agricultural, or industrial wastewater. A techno-economic assessment of ECS at scales sufficient to meet localized fertilizer demand estimated breakeven prices of US$8.70/kg N for ammonium sulfate, US$9.69/kg N for ammonium nitrate, and US$31.18/kg N for monoammonium phosphate, and US$12.15/kg N for diammonium phosphate. Integration of the techno-economic model with geospatial analysis found ECS-derived fertilizer prices ranged from 2.2x-5.5x local 2016-2026 retail prices, with ECS performing most competitively in the Pacific U.S. region. Sensitivity analysis showed improving current efficiency, increasing current density, lowering capital cost, and increasing equipment lifetime would have the greatest impact on approaching retail cost parity. This work elucidates pathways and barriers to widespread implementation of wastewater-derived fertilizers and advances United Nations Sustainable Development goals for responsible consumption and production, clean water, and zero hunger.
papers.title: Techno-Economic and Geospatial Assessment of Distributed Fertilizer Production via Wastewater Ammonia Solar Electrochemical Stripping

papers.abstract: Naturally evolved light-harvesting complexes are assembled from highly evolutionarily-conserved sequences of amino acids that form functional chemical pockets for chromophores. The protein environment surrounding the chromophore influences its dynamical structure, which can have consequences for light harvesting efficiency. Here, we explore the impact of the C-phycocyanin protein scaffold on the dynamical structure and photoexcited states of the phycocyanobilin (PCB) chromophore using a combination of molecular dynamics and the ab initio Bethe Salpeter equation approach. We compute low-lying excited states of the PCB chromophore for an ensemble of snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, and use a normal mode analysis to understand the nature of thermal displacements of PCB in the confined protein environment. We analyze the excited state energies in terms of one electron and electron-hole contributions, identifying displacement patterns with the strongest exciton-vibrational coupling. Our results provide insight into how thermal motion of the chromophore is altered in protein environments and the resulting impact on photo-excited states, with implications for other natural light harvesting materials.
papers.title: Dynamical confinement effects on chromophore photoexcitations in a light-harvesting protein

papers.abstract: Dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-HT) are neurotransmitters whose dysregulation is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. The influence of single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) chirality on sensing remains underexplored. Mixed-chirality SWC- NTs can limit sensor reproducibility and accuracy. Precise control of electrode material structure may promote more specific surface-analyte interactions, enhancing selectivity. Here, screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCE) were modified with four SWCNT types: mixed-chirality metallic/semiconducting (m/s), metallic (m), or semiconducting (s) SWCNT, and single-chirality semiconducting (6,5)-SWCNT isolated by aqueous two-phase extraction. Vacuum filtration produced surfactant-free SWCNT layers. Codetection of 5-HT and DA was evaluated using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE gave the largest potential difference (∆E = Ep(5-HT)− Ep(DA)) of 151 ± 4 mV and a peak current ratio (Ip(DA)/Ip(5-HT)) of 0.99 ± 0.23. Corresponding values for unmodified SPCE, m/s-SWCNT/SPCE, m-SWCNT/SPCE, and s-SWCNT/SPCE were 139±10, 145±3, 143±6, and 147±3 mV, and 0.60±0.23, 0.63±0.12, 0.63±0.11, and 0.69±0.01, respectively. The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE detected both analytes even when one analyte was present in excess. Between 0.04 and 1 µM, linear responses were obtained for 5-HT alone, DA in the presence of 1 µM 5-HT, and 5-HT in the presence of 1 µM DA, with sensitivities of 0.024 ± 0.002, 0.011 ± 0.001, and 0.024± 0.001 nA/nM, respectively. These results show that SWCNT chirality control improves the electrochemical co-detection of 5-HT and DA.
papers.title: Single-chirality single-walled carbon nanotubes for electrochemical co-detection of serotonin and dopamine

papers.abstract: 2 ABSTRACT Modern peptide drug discovery combines mRNA display-derived libraries and iterative optimization of hits using solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) during hit-to-lead process. Part of this discovery workflow is the need for sufficient amounts of high-quality peptide targets, free from impurities to support the required preclinical assays. In this context, there is a need for streamlined high throughput purification (HTP) workflow coupled with high throughput analytical assays, enabling faster analysis of large volumes of synthetic peptide libraries for purification to accelerate the discovery process. We have developed and validated an ultra-high throughput (uHT) acoustic ejection mass spectrometry (AEMS) based pre-quality control (QC) triage assay for peptide libraries in HTP process, which achieves a sampling rate of ~2 sec/sample with minimal sample requirement (25- 45 µL) and solvent consumption, and fast data analysis, suitable for large sample size in discovery setting. Sample purity profile of the library provided by the newly developed assay is beneficial for HT identification of samples that will or will not advance to purification, enabling a streamlined, faster process, and immediate decisionmaking. Results from the validation and bridging studies are in agreement with the currently employed low-throughput UPLC-UV/MS based HTP pre-QC assay. Integration of the recently developed AEMS-based pre-QC assay in the HTP workflow using a sample purity cut-off of 15% for go/no-go decision renders a minimal false negative, <6% and a false positive results of <12%, making it applicable for the purpose of vetting which samples should be purified to reduce the overall experimental time and cost resource in the HTP process. The recently developed assay demonstrated the first application of AEMS as a pre-QC step in peptide HTP workflow, and its potential application for broad peptide library screening in drug discovery.
papers.title: Integration of Acoustic Ejection Mass Spectrometry Enables Efficient High Throughput Purification Workflow for Peptides in Discovery Space

papers.abstract: Low efficiency in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) is often blamed on charge balance, yet the device models that could test this are rarely converged or constrained by measured inputs. We solve converged drift–diffusion, transfermatrix and dipole models for three deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) phosphine-oxide hosts, S1, S3 and S4, with an open solver verified against a converged commercial reference, and we constrain every hostspecific input by measurement: film optical constants from ellipsometry, film photoluminescence, voltammetric host levels and host transport fitted to quality-gated single-carrier current–voltage data. In every converged model OLED with the fitted transport, and also with a shallow-trap transport alternative and with offsets across their identifiable range, charge balance and host confinement are not the limit. What decides the efficiency is where the recombination zone sits: moving it from the electron-transport interface into the host raises the computed air outcoupling about threefold. The model-conditioned efficiency ceiling is therefore set by zone placement and by the photoluminescence quantum yield, which also fixes the host ranking S1>S4≳S3, and transport engineering becomes an outcoupling lever. Two measurements, thickness-dependent current–voltage and angle-resolved photoluminescence, would pin the remaining model ranges (all device quantities are model outputs).
papers.title: Recombination-zone position, not charge balance, sets the efficiency ceiling of deep-blue TADF host OLEDs

papers.abstract: Self-derived phase engineering of metal oxides offers a powerful route to create interfaces without introducing foreign metallic elements, yet achieving systematic control over phase transition remains challenging. Here, active nitrogen-mediated phase engineering was demonstrated across various metal oxides (SnO 2 , ZnO, and TiO 2 ). As a model biphasic material, Sn/SnO 2 was investigated where urea thermolysis enabled the progressive formation of metallic Sn while largely preserving the host structure, allowing the Sn0 fraction to be systematically controlled. Temperature-programmed experiments using mass spectrometry and FT-IR revealed the involvement of nitrogen-containing intermediates during urea decomposition and supported their central role in driving phase engineering of SnO 2 . Density functional theory (DFT) based calculations on a Sn/SnO 2 model constructed using a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) revealed electron transfer from metallic Sn to SnO 2 and the resulting redistribution of surface electron density. The resulting self-derived Sn/SnO 2 biphasic material yields favorable surface chemistry by altered surface oxygen behavior and reactivity translating directly into two applications: enhanced chemoresistive formaldehyde gas sensing under humid conditions with ppb-level detection, as well as improved formate production in electrochemical CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR). Our results identify active nitrogen as a chemical handle for regulating oxide partial reduction and provide a general framework for the systematic engineering of metal/oxide interfaces.
papers.title: Self-Derived Metal/Oxide Interface Engineering via Active Nitrogen Mediation

papers.abstract: Outcoupling designs for organic light-emitting diodes rest on the complex refractive index of every layer, yet host films are often given a constant index without absorption. We show what measured constants change, and what they do not. Variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films (S1, S3 and S4), refitted from the raw data with several dispersion models, pins the index of the S1 and S4 films to a model-andspot spread of about ±0.002 (about ±0.004 at 95% once substrate-oxide, incidence-angle and roughness systematics are propagated) and reveals a weak absorption tail in S4 that follows its triphenylamine-centered lowest singlet transition; the S3 film is bracketed. Propagated through a dipole model of a deep-blue stack in which the neat host film is the emitter, the measured constants leave the design itself (best emitter position, optimum electron-transport-layer thickness) unchanged within a few nanometers but shift the predicted outcoupling by up to 14% relative (15.1 against 17.2% at the optimum, about 2 percentage points), with the blue dispersion of the index and, for S4, the absorption tail in the emission band contributing comparably (up to about 7% each). Emitter orientation and the emitter–cathode distance act far more strongly, by factors of 2 to 5. Both films are close to isotropic, yet the calculated transition dipoles of S3 and S4 lie in the molecular plane, so growing these hosts with flat-lying molecules is the clearest route to higher outcoupling, worth about a factor of two in the model.
papers.title: Measured Host Optical Constants Shift Deep-Blue OLED Outcoupling by up to 14% (Relative) While Leaving the Stack Design Intact

papers.abstract: Delayed-fluorescence rates and their temperature laws are how thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials are ranked, yet the rate law is usually fixed before the analysis, and flash-lamp decays mix the emission with the excitation profile. We show that weak-form regression, with photon-counting statistics and the excitation built into its features, identifies the rate law as a sequence of linear problems with calibrated uncertainties. With a known pulse the whole record, including the excitation window, is used; otherwise the emission after the window is tested against first-order, bimolecular and dispersive terms, and temperature laws are ranked by bootstrap selection frequency. On synthetic decays with lifetimes of 1–1000 µs the method approaches the expected-Fisher precision benchmark and, with the full covariance of its weak residuals, matches fullrecord Poisson maximum likelihood on identical data, whereas ignoring the excitation tail biases rates by more than an order of magnitude and creates spurious activation in more than half of temperature-independent series. Applied to two deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts, it shows that the later-window delayed emission is not purely first order and that its effective rate has no resolved thermal activation between 200 and 300 K. For this effective rate the tested single-gap Marcus law with the computed gaps is ruled out as rate limiting, which points to a temperature-independent or smallbarrier channel. An identifiability map and open code let any laboratory check, before reporting, which rate law its instrument can resolve.
papers.title: Weak-Form Regression Recovers the Delayed-Fluorescence Rate Law from Flash-Lamp Decays with Near-Optimal Precision

papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) is increasingly used to answer biological questions, yet effective collaboration between mass spectrometrists and researchers in other fields can be limited by differences in terminology, expectations, and familiarity with analytical workflows. This review provides a practical and accessible guide to incorporating MS into biological and environmental research with an emphasis on improving communication and collaboration. In the review, we walk through the MS workflow including defining the scientific question, selecting an analytical approach, sample collection and preparation, instrumental analysis, data processing, quality assessment, and interpretation. Particular attention is given to concepts that commonly create confusion across fields, including quantitative strategies, analytical controls, sample handling, instrument monitoring, and data reporting expectations. We also discuss the respective roles of both experimentalists and mass spectrometrists throughout the research process and highlight areas where early communication can prevent downstream problems. To support real-world application, the review includes a glossary of commonly used MS terminology and a checklist of key considerations for collaborative studies. Together, these resources are intended to make MS workflows more approachable and to foster the kind of scientific symbiosis between researchers and mass spectrometrists that is needed to generate high-quality, interpretable, and meaningful data.
papers.title: Scientific Symbiosis: Bridging Expertise and Fostering Effective Collaborations with Mass Spectrometrists

papers.abstract: Solutions of 5’-methoxy-1’,3’,3’-trimethyl-6-nitrospiro[chromene-2,2’-indoline] in alcohols are intensely pink in the dark, become colorless under white light and recover their color thermally, with Arrhenius activation energies of 101.1± 0.5, 104.9± 1.6 and 105.3± 1.4 kJ mol−1 in ethanol, methanol and acidified ethanol, respectively. The measured process is therefore the thermal formation of the merocyanine (MC) from the photogenerated spiropyran (SP). The absorbance of the equilibrated ethanol solution, combined with the calculated oscillator strength, indicates that MC constitutes only a small fraction of the compound, of the order of a few per cent. With continuum solvation alone no cis-merocyanine intermediate (TCC) is found, whereas in a complex with five explicit ethanol molecules a fast SP⇌TCC pre-equilibrium precedes a considerably slower isomerization to the trans isomer (TTC). The reversible kinetic model shows that the measured rate constant reflects the position of the
papers.title: Thermal Formation of a Magenta Merocyanine in Ethanol: A Microsolvated SP→TCC→TTC Pathway in a Nitrospiropyran

papers.abstract: Background. Computational prediction of compound–target associations can help prioritize hypotheses for experimental investigation. While deep learning architectures are increasingly proposed, their apparent superiority often relies on comparisons against untuned classical baselines or evaluation protocols prone to data leakage. Objective. We present a scaffold-disjoint evaluation benchmark derived from ChEMBL 37 to evaluate multitask neural representations against tuned classical similarity search, and we investigate whether combining both paradigms yields improved ranking performance. Methods. The benchmark comprised 100,000 compounds, 1,979 human single-protein targets, and 139,789 positive associations, partitioned by Bemis–Murcko scaffold into train (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) sets. All hyperparameters were selected on the validation set. We compared a multitask MLP with a tuned K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN-20) baseline, as well as a hybrid model integrating both representations. Results. On the held-out test set, the tuned KNN-20 achieved a Hits@10 of 0.9335, statistically indistinguishable from the 10-seed multitask MLP ensemble (0.9355; Δ = +0.0021, 95% CI [−0.0012,+0.0052]). However, a hybrid model integrating both representations (40% KNN, 60% MLP) achieved a significantly higher Hits@10 of 0.9426, outperforming both KNN-20 (Δ = +0.0091, 95% CI [+0.0066,+0.0116]) and the MLP alone (Δ = +0.0070, 95% CI [+0.0052,+0.0089]). Conclusions. Our results demonstrate that while complex neural models do not inherently outperform well-tuned classical baselines, they capture complementary information. A hybrid approach combining classical chemical similarity and multitask neural representations yields a modest but statistically significant improvement in ranking performance within this benchmark. This study emphasizes the necessity of rigorous baseline tuning and suggests hybrid architectures as a promising direction for compound–target prediction.
papers.title: Integrating classical similarity and multitask neural representations

papers.abstract: Atomically precise thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters are used in catalysis, sensing and nanomedicine, where thermal activation, reaction conditions or local heating can change their atomic structure. Whether the gold–thiolate shell remains a fixed protective layer at elevated temperature, or takes part in the restructuring of the cluster, is still an open question, because first-principles molecular dynamics is limited to small clusters and short times. Here we train MACE-AuSCH, an equivariant machine-learned interatomic potential, on a published density functional theory dataset and validate it against 16 crystallographically characterised clusters (cohesive-energy RMSE of 2.1 meV/atom). We then follow seven Aun(SCH3)m clusters, from Au25 to Au279 and with icosahedral and FCC-derived cores, between 8 and 800 K. In all clusters, the effective stiffness of the Au–S bonds is 3.3 to 7.5 times that of the Au–Au bonds, and the metallic Au–Au network reorganises first while most of the Au–S connectivity is kept. At 500 K, the largest core displacements occur in the FCC-derived Au52 and Au92. At 800 K, Au atoms move in both directions between the metallic core and the staple shell, and the loss of Au–S connectivity generally grows with cluster size, from 3% for Au25 to about 40% for Au144. These results describe the protecting shell as a dynamic reservoir of Au atoms and point to an intracluster route that may precede ligand and metal exchange, fragmentation and sintering.
papers.title: The Thiolate Shell as a Dynamic Gold Reservoir: Size-Dependent Thermal Restructuring of Gold Nanoclusters from MACE-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics

papers.abstract: The CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) covers drug-like molecules through an automated assignment program that types atoms, assigns charges from bond-charge increments, and transfers missing bonded parameters from analogous ones with an associated penalty. The algorithms are published, but the program and its two hand-built rule files are distributed only in binary form. We describe LigandFF, an open-source reimplementation built exclusively from the published algorithms and the public CGenFF 5.0 topology, parameter and charge-increment files. LigandFF implements the published ring, resonance and aromaticity perception, the rule language for atom typing, the bond-charge-increment scheme with peratom charge penalties, the penalty-weighted analogy search, halogen lone pairs, and writes CHARMM stream files, PSF files and OpenMM and GROMACS inputs. Its typing rules were written against the CGenFF training molecules, and its substitution-penalty matrices were fitted to 5,787 analogies that the official program recorded in the parameter file. On held-out test splits, LigandFF types 97.4% and 97.8% of two sets of CGenFF training molecules with every atom correct (99.7% and 99.6% of atoms). Replaying the analogies recorded in the parameter file against the database they were made from, it recovers the official program’s choice of source parameter for 92.1% of 1,447 held-out cases. It reproduces the program-5.0 charges and penalties printed in the CGenFF 5.0 supporting information exactly, and all 2,074 benchmark molecules produce systems that build in OpenMM. All references are CGenFF training molecules or outputs of the official program that are already public; agreement with the official program on new drug-like molecules has not been measured. LigandFF is not the official CGenFF program, and its outputs are labelled accordingly.
papers.title: LigandFF: an open-source implementation of rule-based atom typing, charge assignment and parameter assignment by analogy

papers.abstract: Pt(IV) coordination compounds act as anticancer prodrugs that are intracellularly reduced to cytotoxic Pt(II) species, a process whose selectivity and kinetics depend critically on the nature of the axial leaving (L L ) and bridging (L B ) ligands. Using DFT/IEFPCM calculations in water, we examined the ascorbate-mediated reduction of six [PtIV(NH 3 ) 2 Cl 2 (L L )(L B )] complexes bearing different axial-ligand combinations of chloride, bromide, and dichloroacetate (DCA): L L /L B = Br/Cl, Cl/Cl, DCA/Cl, as well as DCA/Br, Cl/Br, and Br/Br. For the full series, the mechanistic analysis was therefore focused on the inner-sphere pathway involving nucleophilic attack of the ascorbate enolate at the C β center (M2), characterized as concerted yet highly asynchronous. Both axial ligands modulate the activation barrier, charge-transfer efficiency, and Pt-L bond dissociation, but the bridging ligand exerts the dominant effect: L B = chloride derivatives display the highest free-energy barriers (Δ[Δ ‡ G298] ≈ 2-4 kcal mol -1 ), high charge-transfer percentages (49%-50%) and later transition states relative to L B = bromide analogs. Additionally, the activation barrier is most strongly associated with the extent of charge transfer and its coupling to C β –L B bond formation, rather than the overall bond-structural event. These results suggest that L B primarily determines the dissociative-reduction behavior, while L L provides secondary control, thereby providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how axial-ligand combinations influence redox latency in Pt(IV) scaffolds.
papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ascorbate-Mediated Activation of Pt(IV) Prodrugs: Axial-Ligand Modulation of Dissociative Reduction Pathways and Redox Latency

papers.abstract: Dynamic material arrays that combine programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout could enable materials that both adapt their spatial organization and represent molecular information. DNA nanotechnology offers exceptional control over nanoscale organization, yet most DNA-templated material arrays are static, whereas dynamic DNA circuits typically rely on indirect ensemble readouts. Here, we present a Reconfigurable Material Display, implemented as REMBRANDT (REconfigurable Material-Based Representation of Addressable Nanoscale Display sTates), a DNA-origami platform that decouples structural assembly from programmable organization of nanoscale cargo. A 5 × 5 array of independently addressable DNA pixels organizes DNA-functionalized nanocargo, including gold nanoparticles, quantum dots, and ferritin, and programmably relocates them without reconstructing the underlying scaffold. Pixel encodings define programmable single- and multi-material display states, whereas DNA strand-displacement reactions rewrite cargo-pixel associations to produce sequential and reversible display-state transformations. Each display state is directly resolved by atomic force microscopy and electron microscopy at single-particle and single-display resolution. Programmable cargo relocation further visualizes predefined matrix operations as dynamically reconfigurable material patterns. By integrating programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout, REMBRANDT establishes a material display in which molecular information is represented, updated, and visualized through nanocargo organization.
papers.title: Reconfigurable Nanoscale Material Display

papers.abstract: The radical Smiles–Truce rearrangement is a powerful strategy for constructing aryl–carbon bonds, although competing ortho addition often limits the utility of conventional S(VI) sulfonamide precursors. Here, we demonstrate that switching to S(IV) sulfinamides enables selective ipso aryl migration while providing a stereochemical handle for asymmetric induction. We report a visible-light-driven nitrogen-centered radical cascade that converts alkene-tethered N-acyl sulfinamides into densely functionalized lactams, fused bicycles, and spirocycles through a desulfinylative Smiles–Truce rearrangement. The transformation accommodates electronically diverse arenes, heteroarenes, and substituted alkenes, affording products in up to 85% yield. Moreover, enantioenriched sulfinamide precursors enable efficient transfer of stereochemical information to the products, with up to 93% enantiospecificity. In contrast to analogous S(VI) sulfonamide reactions, competing ortho dearomatization is not observed. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the S(IV) system disfavors the competing ortho-addition pathway, providing a mechanistic basis for the observed selectivity reversal and establishing sulfinamides as versatile precursors for stereocontrolled radical annulations.
papers.title: Sulfur Oxidation State Controls Radical Smiles–Truce Rearrangements through a Switch in Cyclization Selectivity

papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven and computationally designed metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) raises a fundamental question: which hypothetical structures are most likely to be experimentally realized? Here, we develop a physicochemically informed strategy to prioritize MOFs for synthesis by integrating molecular synthetic accessibility, framework geometry, electronic structure, solvent removal stability, and thermodynamic stability through positive–unlabeled learning. Using 9,033 experimentally reported MOFs as examples of realized structures and hypothetical MOFs as candidates with unknown synthesizability, we identify 5 complementary physicochemical descriptors that enable effective prioritization, achieving a source-averaged normalized positive rank of 0.93 by placing experimentally realized MOFs near the top of candidate rankings across held-out database sources. Further analysis reveals that experimentally realized MOFs are enriched at low linker geometric distortion and low energy above the convex hull of competing phases, highlighting complementary geometric and thermodynamic considerations. Moreover, secondary building unit–linker analyses identify specific chemical combinations enriched among highly ranked hypothetical structures. Together, these findings establish a chemically interpretable approach to prioritizing hypothetical MOFs and help bridge the gap between computational materials design and experimental synthesis.
papers.title: Physicochemical Prioritization of Hypothetical Metal–Organic Frameworks for Experimental Synthesis

papers.abstract: DNA-Encoded Libraries (DELs) are indispensable high-throughput platforms in drug discovery, but the widely adopted split-and-pool synthesis method is fundamentally limited: the DNA merely records, rather than directs, the steps of chemistry. This lack of programmatic control imposes mandatory downstream chemistry congruency, restricts structural diversity, and inevitably generates a combinatorial explosion of un-drug-like molecules, hindering both hit-finding and the acquisition of structurally informative data required for machine learning (ML) models. To resolve these core constraints, we developed Programmed DEL Synthesis (PDS), a robust, industrially applicable platform for non-combinatorial DEL construction in which the DNA actively directs the synthesis. PDS is built upon a sort-and-pool mechanism expanded by three key innovations: sequence-specific installation of first building blocks using charged carrier codons, a multinomial encoding strategy that enables libraries exceeding 20 billion unique encodings in three chemical steps, and non-combinatorial germline assembly that allows for the programmatic omission of undesirable building block combinations. We demonstrate the platform with Library i01, a three-step, threepathway library employing 137 trifunctional scaffolds. The design successfully programmed the systematic merging and un-merging of three mutually incompatible reaction pathways: Acid→Aldehyde→Amine, Amine→Aldehyde→Acid, and Aldehyde→Acid→Amine within a single synthesis. Pilot affinity selections against Carbonic Anhydrase (BCA-II) validated the high fidelity of DNA encoding and efficient building block installation across all steps and pathways, confirming the platform's robust utility for selection. PDS transforms chemical congruency and drug-likeness into programmable properties, offering a precise, efficient solution that improves library quality without sacrificing chemical space. Crucially, PDS enables the construction of structurally tailored 2nd Generation DELs needed to provide the high-resolution data required for productive ML-driven active learning cycles, establishing a critical operational link for modern drug development.
papers.title: DNA Directed Chemistry: Scalable Programmed DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis for More Chemically Diverse and Drug-Like Libraries

papers.abstract: Engineering charge separation and recombination through non-covalent interactions offers a powerful route to functional photoactive materials without the need for covalent re-engineering. Here, we investigate the ultrafast excited-state dynamics of host-guest complexes formed between a valinol-bridged perylene diimide (PDI) dimer macrocycle and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) guests using sub-50 femtosecond time resolution transient absorption spectroscopy. Macrocycle complexation with pyrene, perylene, and coronene introduces efficient charge-transfer pathways absent in the free host. Photoexcitation of the PDI dimer host leads to rapid quenching of stimulated emission and sub-picosecond formation of PDI radical anions, providing direct evidence for ultrafast hole transfer from the excited host to the PAH guest. The resulting charge-separated states persist for hundreds of picoseconds to nanoseconds before recombination. Analysis within the Marcus framework reveals that charge separation proceeds in a near-barrierless regime, whereas charge recombination lies deep in the Marcus inverted region, accounting for long-lived radical pair states. These results establish aromatic guest binding as a non-covalent handle for accessing fast hole transfer enabling long-lived charge-separated states in supramolecular donor-acceptor assemblies, relevant to light harvesting, photoredox catalysis and organic electronics.
papers.title: Ultrafast Charge Separation Controlled by Aromatic Guests in a Perylene Dimer

papers.abstract: The insufficient X-ray scattering contrast and similar neutron scattering cross-sections of Fe and Ni render the accurate determination of ‘coloring scheme’ ambiguous in the vacancy ordered 4 3 −superstructure of CsCl-related phase Fe 1.5 Ni 1.5 Ga 4 . Therefore, to overcome this limitation, X-ray resonance diffraction near the K-absorption edge of Fe has been utilized for the accurate site occupancy pattern of Fe and Ni in the structure of Fe 1.5 Ni 1.5 Ga 4 . Measurements on three independently annealed samples with progressively longer annealing times revealed no evidence of atomic ordering, instead, Fe prefers to partially occupy the Ni site (48𝑔 Wyckoff site) in the structure of binary Ni 3 Ga 4 (𝐼𝑎3̅𝑑 space group, 𝑎 =11.52 Å). The vacancy ordering present at the 16𝑏 site drives the lattice distortion in the structure. Upon heating to ~955 K, the room-temperature (RT) structure transforms to the 2.9 Å CsCl-type structure (𝑃𝑚3̅𝑚 space group), where Fe, Ni and vacancy are randomly distributed suppressing the lattice distortions. DFT based calculations on the hypothetical ordered model predict a ferromagnetic ground state with non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic states lying very close to it in energy. This near-degeneracy points to a highly complex magnetic energy landscape with competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, which explains the experimentally observed spin-glass behavior.
papers.title: Order-Disorder Phase Transitions and Site Occupancy Pattern in Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4 Unravelled by Resonant Scattering
Controlling Interfacial and Bulk Charge Transport in Exsolution Catalysts for High-Activity Water Oxidation

papers.abstract: A molecular property or reaction-yield model is useful to a chemist only when it is right on the query in front of them, yet a model’s uncertainty is rarely checked on chemistry it has not seen. We tested an accept-or-abstain protocol in which a gate, scoring each query by its similarity to the training set and by ensemble spread, returns a prediction only when it accepts the query. The gate’s threshold is set by Learn-then-Test to a target precision on a calibration fold held out by chemistry rather than at random. On public data (23,401 logP values from SangsterLogP with two overlapping external sets, and the Buchwald–Hartwig and Suzuki–Miyaura high-throughput yield datasets), we evaluated eight held-out tests against four hypotheses defined in advance. Ranking queries by the gate’s score lowered the error rate at 30% coverage by 0.16 to 0.35 on seven of the eight tests. At a target precision of 0.8, the calibration fold mattered most for yields: gates calibrated on a random fold accepted almost every reaction with an unseen additive at a precision of 0.59 to 0.75, whereas gates calibrated on held-out additives reached a pooled precision of 0.85 to 0.87 on three of the four tests, at lower coverage. At a target of 0.9, random-fold gates came within 0.05 of the target on three of the four tests. For the random forest, fusing similarity with spread did no better than spread alone, and conformal intervals calibrated on a random fold lost coverage under shift (down to 0.64). On a fluorinated-compound hold-out, the fused score ranked errors no better than chance at 30% coverage, and the held-out-calibrated gate missed its target. All four hypotheses therefore failed their success criteria. In an exploratory analysis, conformal intervals calibrated on the held-out fold recovered coverage on seven of the eight tests, at the cost of wider intervals. We release the protocol, the code and the complete results.
papers.title: Accept or abstain? A pre-specified test of reliability gates calibrated on held-out chemistry for molecular property and reaction-yield models

papers.abstract: Machine-learning models for enantioselectivity on polysaccharide chiral stationary phases increasingly report high accuracy, but almost always under random data splits. We re-examined this problem on CMRT, the largest public chiral chromatography dataset, curating it into 10,525 enantiomer pairs covering 530 DOI groupsand25columns.Underatrueleave-one-paper-outprotocol,elution-orderaccuracyfallsfrom 66.1 % under a random split to 52.9 %, indistinguishable from a within-paper permutation null (52.3 % ± 0.6). Between-paper variance accounts for 38.5 % of the total variance, but it cannot be predicted from compositional features, so domain adaptation is ineffective. The molecular signal is real within a single paper (median per-paper correlation r = +0.185) but falls to r = +0.0009 for an unseen paper, and adding trainingpapersdoesnothelp.Avariancedecompositionofasingle-laboratorygridshowsthatonly 23.05 % of the variance is attributable to additive main effects of molecule and condition, the remaining 76.95 % being an unidentifiable molecule × condition interaction and noise. We therefore argue that the bottleneck liesnotinmodelcapacityordescriptorqualitybutinthedatastructure:adding condition metadata,buildingsystematicmolecule×conditiongrids,introducingreplicatemeasurementsand recording failed separations are the prerequisites for improving transferability.
papers.title: Where machine learning for enantioselectivity on polysaccharide chiral stationary phases actually fails: a leave-one-paper-out reappraisal of 10,525 enantiomer pairs

papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are generally described by their pristine structures, although aqueous use and release expose them to ligands and dissolved ions that can reconstruct their coordination chemistry before biological contact. Here, we follow HKUST-1 across an environmental-to-biological exposure cascade using complementary X-ray methods. Time-resolved Cu K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy (EXAFS) showed rapid, matrix-specific disruption of the Cu-carboxylate paddlewheel in borehole water (BHW) and serum-free cell-culture medium (CCM). In XANES linear-combination fitting (LCF), the spectral fraction represented by pristine HKUST-1 became unresolved in BHW by 24 h and decreased to 4.1% in CCM by 4 h. The transformed solids were represented predominantly by carbonate-/hydroxide-like Cu environments in BHW and phosphate-, CuCl-, and CuO-reference-like environments in CCM. Powder X-ray diffraction, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, Cu Kβ valence-to-core X-ray emission spectroscopy, carbon K-edge X-ray Raman scattering, and electron microscopy showed that transformation extended from the Cu ligand field to BTC carboxylate coordination, medium- and long-range order, and morphology. CCM generated operational <0.02 µm Cu at an initial rate of µg mL-1 h-1, compared with µg mL-1 h-1 in BHW, yet low sustained Cu mobilization in BHW did not indicate persistence of the parent framework. On a nominal material-mass basis, BHW aging increased apparent acute potency toward Daphnia magna, lowering the 48 h EC50 from 0.54 to 0.18 µg mL-1. Cryogenic X-ray fluorescence mapping and spatially resolved XANES showed further Cu re-coordination during gastrointestinal transit. Following pristine-material exposure, the HKUST-1-like contribution decreased from 10.7% in the foregut to 0.2% in the hindgut, whereas 86–98% of the Cu signal following BHW-aged-material exposure was represented by non-HKUST-1 environments throughout the gut. Framework disruption is therefore followed by matrix-selected reconstruction and biological ligand exchange. MOF performance and environmental health depend on the exposure-conditioned material, not on pristine structure or dissolved-metal concentration alone.
papers.title: Matrix-dependent transformation governs the chemical identity and biological fate of a metal–organic framework

papers.abstract: Jev and Clef outperform a released ChemBERT classifier supervised on the Organic Synthesis Procedures with Argument Roles (OSPAR) corpus on a human-adjudicated Creative Commons (CC) synthesis reference. With supplied mention spans, 17 procedures provide 288 resolved operation–candidate pairs: the positive-role micro-averaged F1 score (the precision–recall harmonic mean) is 96.59% for Jev, 95.27% for Clef and 90.36% for ChemBERT. Fixed role definitions are used without prompt demonstrations or author-performed task-specific fine-tuning; prior OSPAR-based prompt development is disclosed. A new retrospective evaluation applies the same configurations and scoring to 258 pairs from 11 OSPAR test procedures, yielding 97.92, 94.64 and 97.38%, respectively. Clef’s point-estimate ordering relative to ChemBERT therefore changes between corpora. These OSPAR procedures were previously viewed during development, so the extension supplies a matched source-corpus comparison rather than untouched validation. A fresh CC repeat is reported separately. Reference-convention and sentence-boundary sensitivities clarify the scope of the CC advantage. Clef-flash reaches 78.96% in the original CC evaluation, with negative-pair rejection limiting precision. Separately, ChemBERT’s CC exact-span and joint-relation F1 are 84.42 and 74.61%. The study demonstrates strong role assignment without additional task training while separating corpus dependence, rejection and mention recovery from complete synthesis extraction.
papers.title: Schema-guided zero-shot decision models for chemical synthesis argument roles: comparison with supervised ChemBERT

papers.abstract: Natural products (NPs) have a major impact on several research areas, including drug discovery and development, food and agricultural chemistry, and the cosmetic industry. Annotated compound databases of NPs provide a structured and organized framework that facilitates access to information, particularly if the compound database is freely available. Over the past few years, a compound library from eight countries, called the Latin American Natural Product Database (LANaPDB), has been assembled, curated, and annotated and currently contains 14,741 unique compounds. The compounds are annotated with extensive bioactivity data retrieved from the peer-reviewed literature, along with structural information (e.g., chirality, taxonomic and structural classification), accessibility (commercial availability or estimated synthetic feasibility), and other properties of interest in drug discovery. Although all the information in LANaPDB is in the public domain and documented in the peer-reviewed literature, it was not available through a free website that enabled rapid and intuitive access to all the information. The goal of this manuscript is to introduce and describe a freely available web server dedicated to systematically and intuitively exploring the contents of LANaPDB. The website provides a dynamic interface that spans from basic to advanced structural and information search, multi-parameter filtering, interactive visualization of phylogenetic and chemotaxonomic diversity, geographical mapping of compound origins, and molecular structure rendering. It is also possible to download the entire compound database from the website. The website facilitates the exploration of Latin American NPs and multidisciplinary research. The web-based platform of LANaPDB is https://www.lanapdb.com/.
papers.title: LANaPDB: A web-based platform for the Latin American Natural Product Database

papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular pathways underlying light-driven reactions is essential for developing efficient and sustainable photochemical processes. Here, we investigate the photoinduced dynamics and reactivity of deprotonated 4-nitrothiophenol (4-NTP) in aqueous solution using transient nitrogen and oxygen K-edge near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT) and equation-of-motion coupled-cluster (EOM-CC) calculations. Valence-state calculations identify the lowest bright excited state S1 as a ππ∗ state with partial charge-transfer character, consistent with the experimentally observed absorption maximum near 408 nm. Following excitation at 343 nm, transient NEXAFS reveals the formation and reaction pathways of both singlet and triplet excited states. The combined experimental and theoretical results indicate that intersystem crossing proceeds from the vibrationally hot S1 state through the higher-lying T2 state, followed by rapid internal conversion to T1. The S1 state additionally undergoes photodissociation on the nanosecond timescale, producing NO2 and a thiophenyl radical. In parallel, the T1 state reacts with dissolved O2, leading to formation of the 4-NTP radical and reactive oxygen species, including hydroxyl radicals. oxygen K-edge measurements provide direct evidence for the formation and persistence of these oxygen-centered reactive intermediates. These results establish distinct singlet-and triplet-mediated reaction channels in aqueous 4-NTP and demonstrate the capability of elementspecific transient X-ray spectroscopy, supported by high-level EOM-CC calculations, to resolve competing excited-state pathways and photochemical reactions in solution.
papers.title: Excited-state dynamics and photo-reaction pathways of 4-nitrothiophenol in solution investigated by time-resolved soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy

papers.abstract: A mechanistic DFT study with explicit Et2O microsolvation and microkinetic modeling unveils how organomagnesium reagents (nBuMgX, X = Cl, Br, nBu) undergo structural reorganization during nitrile additions, generating aggregates that hamper reactivity. Starting from halide-bridged dimers (Et2O)·nBuMg(µ-X)2MgnBu·(Et2O), nitrile addition proceeds via a bimetallic 6-centered transition state (∆G‡ ∼ 19 kcal mol−1) and yields imido-bridged products stabilized by more than 30 kcal mol−1. For mixed reagents (X = Cl, Br), post-nucleophilic addition Schlenk equilibria lead to di-imido dimers (Et2O)·XMg(µ-[N])2MgX·(Et2O) along with the initial reactive dimer. In contrast, starting from the homoleptic nBu2Mg, post-nucleophilic addition equilibria deliver a Mg-based tetramer Mg4(µ-[N])4nBu4 that scavenges nucleophilic groups. Engaging the remaining Mg–alkyl bonds in such a tetramer requires overcoming an overall energy barrier of 27 kcal mol−1, thus limiting conversion. Microkinetic simulations, based on computed free energy profiles and experimental initial conditions, quantitatively reproduce the experimental 50% conversion plateau and 4:1 product:side product ratio, establishing aggregation-driven inhibition as the origin of incomplete reactivity. These findings provide rational guidelines for optimizing Grignard transformations through reagent selection, additive strategies and solvation engineering, with applications for polyolefin upgrading and pharmaceutical synthesis.
papers.title: Aggregation-Driven Self-Inhibition of Grignard Reagents: Insights from DFT and Microkinetic Modeling

papers.abstract: Ruthenium catalysts prepared by deposition–precipitation (DP) contain highly hydrated oxidized Ru species whose structure and evolution remain difficult to define. Here, Ru catalysts supported on alumina and two activated carbons were investigated to clarify how support chemistry and water content affect the Ru phase formed by DP. HR-TEM, O K-edge NEXAFS, H2-TPR and CO chemisorption reveal marked support-dependent differences in Ru aggregation, local oxygen coordination, reducibility and site accessibility. On alumina, hydrated Ru oxy-hydroxide species coexist with RuO2-like local domains, whereas carbon supports stabilize predominantly hydroxylated and structurally disordered Ru environments. Post-synthesis drying and ageing progressively alter these properties through dehydration, with markedly different consequences depending on the support. On alumina, water removal promotes structural consolidation and RuO2-like ordering, making the Ru(IV) → Ru(III) → Ru(0) reduction sequence kinetically resolvable while decreasing the population of accessible Ru sites. On activated carbons, dehydration mainly affects site accessibility without inducing comparable RuO2-like ordering. Catalytic transfer hydrogenolysis of diphenyl ether (DPE) provides a first catalytic assessment of these differences: DPE conversion follows the same trend as CO-accessible Ru sites, while aromatic yield does not increase proportionally with activity because consecutive hydrogenation is also promoted. These results identify water as a transient structural component of DP-derived Ru catalysts and show that drying and storage history are integral to controlling their reducibility, site accessibility and catalytic behavior.
papers.title: Drying, ageing and reducibility of Ru catalysts obtained via deposition-precipitation: the hidden role of water

papers.abstract: Out-of-phase boundary (OPB) defects are a hallmark of spiral-driven growth in Aurivillius phase thin films, often arising from screw dislocation-mediated layer propagation. These boundaries are associated with localised strain gradients and modify polarisation and diffraction responses. Existing analytical XRD models that treat OPBs as planar or parallel features have limitations in capturing the vertical gradient in lattice displacement and the angular asymmetry observed in spiral-grown films. In this work, we introduce a generalised model that represents OPBs as stacked pyramidal defects along the film thickness, as observed in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) cross sections. The model incorporates a three dimensional structure factor formalism that accounts for atomic positions, fractional lattice displacements, the inclination of the OPB boundaries and other parameters. Simulated X-ray diffraction patterns based on this model reproduce the asymmetric peak broadening and splitting observed in Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 thin films with high fidelity and enable a non-destructive estimation of OPB density, and a more realistic description of defect geometry than planar models allow. This work establishes a three-dimensional, predictive framework for spiralmediated OPB defects in layered ferroelectric oxides, offering a basis for defect engineering and materials optimisation in future memory and neuromorphic applications.
papers.title: X-Ray Diffraction Model for Spiral-Growth-Driven Defects in Layered Thin Films

papers.abstract: Literature-mined release curves can support model development while overstating applicability to an unseen publication. We test the consequences of changing the uncertainty unit from a release observation to a formulation and then an entire publication block. A unit-audited public PLGA dataset provides 1-, 3-, and 7day endpoints for 257 formulations from 99 DOI groups. Fixed single-threaded baselines are evaluated with five prespecified 60/20/20 publication train/calibration/test partitions. The primary outcome is simultaneous coverage of every eligible formulation endpoint within a held-out publication. Extra-trees MAE was 0.172 release fraction under publication splitting, versus 0.136 under formulation-random splitting; mean publication-split R2 was 0.002. Pooled-point calibration yielded 68% empirical publication coverage, compared with 88% for publication-max calibration. Mean widths were 0.583 and 0.773, respectively, on a physical 0-1 scale. Additional capacity, feature-block and learning-curve ablations use the same publication holdouts. Only 1.6% of harmonized endpoints coincide with a recorded source time, motivating a resolution audit. Publicationlevel calibration improves empirical simultaneous coverage at the cost of wide intervals; exchangeability and prospective performance remain unestablished.
papers.title: Publication-block calibration reveals wide uncertainty in PLGA release endpoint prediction

papers.abstract: Selecting a polymer nanoparticle solely for tumour accumulation can ignore competing liver uptake. We quantify the relationship between these ranking objectives using paired whole-organ biodistribution measure-ments from the publicly archived Nano-Tumor Database. The primary cohort contains 142 source-labelled Polymeric formulations in 72 connected publication-reference groups, evaluated at 24 hours without temporal extrapolation. Analyses include publication-cluster bootstrap intervals, within-publication active/passive con-trasts, fixed baseline prediction models and prespecified time/material sensitivity analyses. Median tumour and liver accumulation were 0.625%ID and 9.750%ID. Tumour accumulation and the tumour/liver ratio had Spearman correlation 0.561 (publication-bootstrap 95% interval 0.396 to 0.707); only 47.2% of the top-quartile formulations overlapped between objectives. The equal-weight within-publication active/passive log10-ratio contrast was 0.209 (0.091 to 0.325) across 15 overlapping publication groups. Additional objective-weight, publication-omission and capacity ablations preserve the primary cohort. Leave-one-group-out within-publication contrasts range from 0.183 to 0.244 log10 units. The observational contrast remains confounded, and organ selectivity is not a validated safety or efficacy end-point.
papers.title: Tumour accumulation is not tumour-to-liver selectivity: a publication-aware polymer nanoparticle reanalysis

papers.abstract: The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)—the passivating nanometric film that forms on anode surfaces in lithium-ion batteries—remains one of the most critical yet least understood components in electrochemical energy storage. Unraveling its formation, structure, and evolution has proven to be a formidable odyssey, spanning decades of relentless effort and confronting researchers with challenges as daunting as those faced by the ancient voyagers. This review provides a comprehensive, 30-year perspective on this arduous journey, tracing the evolution of computational methods for modeling electrolytes and SEI from early density functional theory (DFT) calculations of isolated molecules to modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) frameworks that promise to accelerate materials discovery. We organize the methodological development into five generations, each representing a milestone in this ongoing voyage: static DFT (1995–2005) establishing thermodynamic foundations; ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) for interfacial dynamics (2005–2010); AIMD integrated with free energy calculations to elucidate electron transfer and rare events (2011–2015); quantitative design rules, space charge effects, and mechanical properties (2016–2020); and advanced DFT techniques combined with MLIPs, generative models, large language models, and self-driving laboratories (2021–2026). We critically assess classical MD, reactive force fields (ReaxFF, eReaxFF), hybrid HAIR methods, kinetic Monte Carlo, and Monte Carlo approaches, demonstrating how each method bridges the chasm between electronic structure and mesoscale phenomena. The review further examines ML applications—from property prediction and spectroscopic signature forecasting to MLIPs achieving first-principles accuracy at classical force-field speeds, generative molecular design, high-throughput screening, active learning, and integration with autonomous experimentation. We identify persistent challenges that continue to test the field’s resolve: long-range electrostatics, transferability across chemical space, time-scale bridging, uncertainty quantification, and data standardization. Practical recommendations for method selection are provided, accompanied by a comprehensive comparative table. This review establishes that the integration of DFT, AIMD, MD, ReaxFF, kMC, MLIPs, and AI has created a powerful multiscale modeling ecosystem, transforming battery research from trial-and-error to rational, data-driven design.
papers.title: Computational Modeling of Electrolytes and the Solid–Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in Li-Ion Batteries: A 30-Year Odyssey from DFT/MD/MC to AI–A Comprehensive Review
Site-preference engineering of cobalt active-site ensembles in spinel oxides for oxygen evolution

papers.abstract: Singlet fission (SF), a multiexciton generation process in organic molecules, offers intriguing possibilities to overcome limitations in multielectron photocatalysis. For this approach to be viable, SF chromophores must combine sufficiently high triplet energies with efficient SF in the polar environments typically required for photocatalytic reactions. Herein, we present a detailed investigation of the excited-state dynamics of a covalently linked dimer based on diphenylhexatriene (DPH), a high-energy SF chromophore, in a polar solvent, benzonitrile (PhCN). While the dimer undergoes SF in toluene, SF is strongly suppressed in PhCN, where the excited-state dynamics instead favour symmetry-breaking charge separation (SBCS). These results highlight solvent polarity as an important consideration in the design of highly symmetric SF chromophores for photocatalytic applications
papers.title: Suppression of Singlet Fission in a DPH dimer by a polar solvent

papers.abstract: AI literacy is increasingly important in undergraduate chemistry education, where students must evaluate generated explanations against chemical principles and evidence. However, the conditions shaping chemistry students’ engagement with AI remain insufficiently understood. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined semi-structured interviews with 36 undergraduate chemistry students from 22 higher education institutions in China. Thematic analysis identified interrelated personal, behavioral, and environmental influences. Participants who expressed confidence in using AI also described selective reliance and deliberate efforts to retain responsibility for academic work. Expected benefits included efficiency and opportunities to ask questions with less perceived interpersonal judgment. Peers and senior students were prominent sources of practical guidance, often preceding formal instruction amid inconsistent institutional expectations. These findings suggest that AI literacy involves self-regulation, affective considerations, and informal social learning. For chemistry educators, they highlight the importance of supporting students’ judgment about AI-assisted explanations, creating space to discuss conceptual uncertainty, and making standards for evaluating chemical claims explicit within peer interactions. The study contributes a qualitative account of how undergraduate chemistry students understand and negotiate AI use within their learning environments.
papers.title: AI Literacy among Undergraduate Chemistry Students from a Social Cognitive Perspective

papers.abstract: This research aims to utilize bioinformatics methods to identify and analyze potential vaccine epitopes for feline calicivirus (FCV). FCV is a highly contagious pathogen causing respiratory illnesses in cats, posing significant challenges due to its genetic variability. The project involved retrieving FCV nucleotide sequences, predicting potential vaccine epitopes, and evaluating their antigenicity, toxicity, and allergenicity. The properties of the vaccine peptide sequence were also predicted and analyzed in 3D. There are 4 identified nucleotide sequences and 5 peptide sequences that show promising attributes of being non-antigenic, non-toxic, and non-allergenic. The methodology employed tools like IEDB, Vaxijen, AllerTOP, ToxinPred, ProtParam, Protein-Sol, SWISS-MODEL, MolProbity website, and PDBsum. Despite the genetic diversity of FCV, targeting conserved regions can potentially provide broad protection. However, further empirical validation through T-cell epitope prediction, secondary structure extrapolation, and molecular docking could be done to ensure vaccine efficacy against emerging FCV strains. Collaborative efforts in veterinary research are also emphasized to expedite vaccine development and implementation.
papers.title: In Silico Design and Structural Validation ofEpitope-Based Vaccine Candidates Against Feline Calicivirus using Immunoinformatics

papers.abstract: Manipulating molecular chirality via strong light–matter coupling holds promise for asymmetric photochemistry and chiral optoelectronics, but a microscopic understanding of how cavity confinement, excitonic delocalization, and vibronic coupling intertwine is still lacking. We address this by simulating the polaritonic absorption and CD spectra of helical perylenediimide (PDI) aggregates in optical cavities, using a generalized Holstein–Tavis–Cummings (HTC) model parametrized from ab initioelectronic-structure calculations and solved with the non-Markovian stochastic Schrödinger equation (NMSSE). Unlike conventional HTC approaches, our model fully incorporates local excitations (LEs), charge-transfer excitations (CTEs), and their mutual couplings. We show that cavity photons generate chiroptical responses beyond the reach of standard exciton theory, yielding strong CD signals even when direct inter-chromophore coupling is negligible. This non-local chiral effect originates from collective coupling to a shared cavity mode, which allows a local excitation to coherently address distant monomers through the quantized field. We further demonstrate that dark polaritonic states are highly sensitive to packing: symmetry breaking via disorder or dipole misalignment lifts their degeneracy into three bright bands. Vibronic coupling, however, broadens the central band and redistributes intensity into sidebands, partially masking the splitting. Together, these findings reveal the microscopic origins of cavity-mediated polaritonic chirality and offer a roadmap for engineering dark states in chiral assemblies.
papers.title: Vibronic Absorption and Circular Dichroism Spectra of Chiral PDI Aggregates in Free Space and Optical Cavities

papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning seeks to explore vast, high-dimensional design spaces, but experimental data are typically sparse and unevenly distributed, limiting generalization beyond observed systems. Molecular thermodynamic property prediction is a prime example. We develop a Physics-guided PC-SAFT neural NETwork, P-SANET, within a reliability-oriented framework integrating physical models, physics-guided target formulation, chemically informed out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation and monotonic error calibration. P-SANET learns the temperature-dependent charging free energy and maps it through PC-SAFT to molecular interaction parameters. This thermodynamically structured target improves prediction accuracy for scaffold-disjoint and structurally novel molecules. A matched-size open-data benchmark further shows that chemically informative coverage, rather than nominal dataset size, is a key determinant of OOD reliability. A monotonic calibrator combining temperature, ensemble uncertainty and embedding novelty provides quantitative error estimates. P-SANET achieves competitive vapor-pressure accuracy against published models and transfers without property-specific retraining to enthalpy of vaporization, liquid density and critical properties.
papers.title: Physics-Guided Learning with Calibrated Uncertainty for Molecular Thermodynamics Beyond Observed Chemical Space

papers.abstract: Recovered oyster shell can be returned to the water as reef substrate, ground into cement-replacing powder, or landfilled, and coastal cities increasingly collect it. Which use is better has not been quantified under uncertainty. A per-tonne, multiobjective Monte Carlo model compares the three uses on living oysters and on net life-cycle carbon relative to disposal. Reef survival is a Bayesian predictive distribution built from four public Billion Oyster Project site counts, used as an external reference only, tested by leaving each site out and by an age-standardized variant. The concrete pathway uses joint draws of cement displacement, service-life ratio and carbon from a companion paper’s model, on a common functional basis with the avoided landfill emission credited once. Per tonne of shell, concrete use changes net carbon by a median -115 kg CO2e (P10–P90 -865 to 624) and is a net saving in 58% of draws, but this depends on durability: -421 kg in the favorable dam case, -120 in the neutral pavement case, +84 in the unfavorable marine case, and a net emission of 1,928 kg against a slag-blended cement. Reef use emits 114 kg and yields 24,533 living oysters (2,394–97,648) per tonne, and costs more carbon than OPC-referenced concrete in 68% of draws. Whether the reef is preferable is a valuation question with a median break-even of 8 g CO2e per living oyster; the share of draws in which sending all shell to the reef is optimal changes by at most 0.10 when any one site is left out. All results are conditional model predictions and not validated environmental benefits.
papers.title: Competing Circular-Economy Uses of Oyster Shell Waste: Uncertainty-Aware Life-Cycle Allocation Between Reef Restoration and Low-Carbon Construction

papers.abstract: Combining stretchability with wireless operation is highly desirable for minimizing mechanical mismatch and reducing the electronic footprint and power burden at dynamic biological interfaces. Yet existing stretchable wireless patches based on passive radio frequency (RF) circuits can sense only physical stimuli that directly alter the resonant circuit, such as pressure, strain, and temperature, leaving no accessible electrical input for electrophysiological or chemical signals and little capacity for local computing function. Here, we realize an active RF circuit architecture using electrochemical transistors that enables both electrode-based sensing, particularly of electrophysiological and biochemical signals, and reservoir edge computing for data compression. This advance addresses the voltage and frequency incompatibility between electrochemical transistors and RF circuits by establishing a previously unexplored operating regime that suppresses ionic responses and, consequently, electrochemical degradation within the channel. Using this architecture, we demonstrate fully implanted cardiac electrogram recording, wound-attached chemical sensing, and wireless reservoir computing for tactile-pattern recognition. Overall, this design substantially expands the capabilities of stretchable wireless platforms to encompass nearly all major sensing modalities together with edge computing.
papers.title: Stretchable Wireless Sensing-Computing Biointerfaces Enabled by High-Voltage Megahertz Electrochemical Transistors

papers.abstract: Microcystins (MC) are a critical class of toxic cyanobacterial secondary metabolites, with specific variants such as MC-LR strictly regulated in drinking water. Despite their extensive structural diversity, comprising over 300 known congeners, comprehensive environmental monitoring is severely hindered by the limited availability of commercial reference standards and public tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra. To address this analytical bottleneck, we developed a non-targeted mass spectrometry-based computational workflow leveraging the Mass Spectrometry Query Language (MassQL) to enable comprehensive MC profiling. By systematically analyzing the chemical space and fragmentation patterns of all MC congeners documented in the CyanoMetDB database, we classified the congeners into nine structurally distinct groups. Subsequently, we designed and optimized a suite of MassQL queries targeting the conserved MC backbone, group-specific motifs, and individual constituent amino acids. The performance of these custom queries was rigorously evaluated following Feature-Based Molecular Networking (FBMN). Application across three independent cyanobacterial bloom datasets comprising both in-house and public data acquired via qTOF and Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry platforms demonstrated highly satisfactory analytical performance based on recall, precision, F1-scores, and Matthews Correlation Coefficients (MCC). We further demonstrated that MassQL functions as a powerful MC candidate prioritization tool orthogonal to molecular networking. By interrogating MS/MS data for specific structural motifs, this query-based approach enabled the discovery and annotation of novel MC congeners lacking public library spectra, significantly enhancing non-targeted screening for water quality and risk assessment.
papers.title: Comprehensive Profiling of Microcystins in Non-Targeted LC-HR-MS Datasets using Mass Spectrometry Query Language (MassQL)

papers.abstract: Precise and consistent reporting of the nucleic acid payload per lipid nanoparticle (LNP) is important for advancing the understanding and development of nanomedicines. However, the reported number of RNA molecules ranges between ∼1-300 in recent investigations. To evaluate the RNA payload across investigations, we introduce and apply a normalized nucleic acid payload metric which accounts for differences in LNP size, nucleotides per RNA and N/P charge ratio. The normalized payload results in a similar value for siRNA-and mRNA-containing LNPs of different LNP sizes, where the average value of 71± 16 nucleotides/zeptoliter agrees well with the expected payload density based on molecular packing arguments. The use of normalized payload harmonizes the reported payload, complements existing payload metrics and enables comparison across samples and measurement techniques at both the single-particle and ensemble-average level.
papers.title: Normalized Nucleic Acid Payload in Lipid Nanoparticles: A Perspective on the Harmonization of Published Data

papers.abstract: Concerted proton-coupled electron transfer (CPET) is central to biological and synthetic energy conversion, yet most studies focus on 1e−/1H+ reactions. The principles governing concerted multi‑proton multi‑electron transfer, as illustrated by water oxidation and CO2 reduction, remain poorly understood. Here, we use femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy to investigate a water-soluble fluoflavine. Following photoexcitation, we resolve an ultrafast branching (<120 fs) from the Franck‑Condon region. One pathway corresponds to concerted 2e−/2H+ transfer (2CPET) from water to fluoflavine and forms a long-lived reduced product; the other produces a short-lived two-electron-reduced intermediate.
